events.title: Anti-MFA: A Writing Workshop for the Rest of Us
events.description: 1 st Sundays from 1 pm to 4 pm at Wolverine Farm Why should the University get to monopolize knowledge, community, and resources? Why should graduate students and professors have all the fun? If we’re going to become serious writers—if we’re going to succeed—we need to come together on a regular basis to read, discuss, and advance our work. Think of this as a step up from a critique group—something with a bit more commitment, consistency, and intention. Each month, writers will submit work for feedback along with some published work for us to read and discuss. Then, each participant will prepare in whatever way they have the desire or capacity for—reading ahead of time, leaving comments, writing a letter, or just showing up the day of. Whatever we end up doing, the point here is to support each other as a community of writers, and what that support looks like is entirely up to you. # # # THIS MONTH’S READING / THEME WE BY LAYLI LONG SOLDIER (GRAYWOLF PRESS, 2026) This Month, we’re going to be reading We by Layli Long Soldier, which is currently longlisted for the National Book Aard, who was just named a MacArthur Fellow, and whose last collection (WHEREAS) won several pretty significant awards. In reading We, we’ll be thinking about “what it means to be in community, to be in relation with family, nation, history, and language. We is the first-person plural, the pronoun of inclusion in English. It is also Wé, the Lakota word meaning “blood”—what is shared and what is shed.” Which is to say: what is our relationship to colonialism; how do we write into this; how much blood has the country shed. We can be purchased around town at Old Firehouse, Perelandra, or other such venues. If buying a book presents an issue, email focopoetlaureate@gmail.com for financial assistance. More information about Layli can be found at https://www.macfound.org/…/ class-of…/layli-long-soldier As always, read or prepare as much or as little as you want, show up even if you haven’t read it, even if you haven’t written anything, etc etc. Meetings: Please note: while this workshop is poetry focused, all genres are welcome. The more the merrier. You also do not have to be a writer or share your own work to participate. Depending on how many people participate, there may not be enough time for everyone to receive feedback. Schedules will be determined from meeting to meeting. Priority will be given to folks who have not received feedback at a previous meeting. If there are a lot of us, we may end up splitting into smaller groups. We’ll just have to see. If you’re interested in participating, email focopoetlaureate@gmail.com or just show up.

events.title: A Mouthful of Blood: Writing the History of the American West A Poetry Workshop presented by the Fort Collins (Co-)Poet Laureate
events.description: About the Workshop The 19th century was as long as they ever come, especially for the United States. Rosy-cheeked and restless after the revolution, America's first centennial witnessed one of the most aggressive, aggrandized campaigns of territorial expansion in modern history, violently displacing Indigenous communities for the sake of empire and land. To return to these texts, as a colonial descendant, is to reckon with the history of America, our fateful inheritance–to interrogate the material circumstances that gave birth to this philosophy of democracy in the first place. (Which, as we have so recently seen, is perhaps something less unimaginable than what has been its reality, from the very beginning.) In this workshop, then, we'll use our unique position and perspective as writers to bring the voices of the past into the present–to channel ourselves, to conduct a kind of necromancy or possession–to see what sort of offering will satisfy these voracious spirits, if they ever could be put to rest. More specifically: attendees will be introduced to an array of primary texts from the 19th century–encompassing treaties and cessions, the gold rush, Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show, congressional debates, military commissions, the railroad, the telegraph, massacres and more–which, utilizing a documentary approach, they'll write into and through. Besides this, attendees will also receive a crash course in the history and practice of documentary poetics–from its progenitors in Muriel Rukeyser, Charles Reznikoff, and Ezra Pound to the modern present. We'll also look to Walt Whitman, the quintessential American poet himself, as a kind of guiding light for our own work–all the better with which we can shadow or eclipse. At the end of the workshop, students will leave with a deeper understanding of the true history of this country, how this might fit in to their own poetic practice, and everything else they might need to usher in the revolution through a new distinctive piece. Please note: while this workshops is focused on poetry, all genres are welcome. No familiarity or experience with historical documents is necessary as well. RSVPs would be appreciated via a quick email to focopoetlaureate@gmail.com The workshop is free. About the Facilitator Jake Friedman (he/him) proudly serves, along with Erica Reid, as a co-Poet Laureate of Fort Collins, CO, which he moved to in 2022 to complete an MFA in Poetry from Colorado State University. Prior to that, he spent eleven years in Phoenix, AZ engaging a variety of artistic and literary endeavors–founding and directing a small press called Four Chambers, serving in progressive administrative positions at the Virginia G. Piper Center for Creative Writing at Arizona State University, and a brief stint as the Community Engagement and Programs Manager for the City of Phoenix Office of Arts and Culture–not to mention reading on grants, serving on boards, and other sundry professional things. Creatively, he has received a number of relatively small but personally significant honors–a University and College Prize from the Academy of American Poets, scholarships from the Community of Writers, and a Finalist for the Just Buffalo Poetry Fellowship. He is currently working on a manuscript that is more or less this class. If there's anything you want to do in terms of literary arts or poetry out here, send him an email at focopoetlaureate@gmail.com .

Priority will be given to folks who have not received feedback at a previous meeting. If there are a lot of us, we may end up splitting into smaller groups. We’ll just have to see. If you’re interested in participating, email focopoetlaureate@gmail.com or just show up.
